x.t: New Zealand bat carefully to draw with India
b: India and New Zealand have finished a long cricket match called a [[test-match|Test match]]. It ended in a [[test-draw|draw]], so nobody won.
India scored a huge 720 runs. To win, they had to get New Zealand's batters out. But New Zealand batted carefully on the last day.
India could not get them out. So the teams agreed to call it a draw. The next match starts on 27 November.

o.t: New Zealand bat out the last day to save the Wellington Test
b: The first [[test-match|Test match]] between India and New Zealand ended in a [[test-draw|draw]] on Monday 23 November, the fifth and final day. It was played at the Basin Reserve in Wellington, New Zealand.

India batted first and made 720 for 9 before they chose to [[declare|declare]], which means ending their innings early. KL Rahul and Rishabh Pant both scored [[century|centuries]], scores of 100 runs or more. New Zealand replied with 368 all out, including 175 not out from Henry Nicholls.

To win, India had to get New Zealand out. Batting again, New Zealand lasted 120 [[over|overs]] and reached 239 for 5. Devon Conway made 65, and Daryl Mitchell (49 not out) and Glenn Phillips (26 not out) held on until the captains agreed to end the match as a draw. The second Test starts at Hagley Oval, Christchurch, on 27 November.

stories.think: What helps a team keep going when the other side is far ahead?

quiz.q: How many runs did India score in their first innings?

x.t: Europe's big rocket waits to fly after a problem on the ground
b: Europe's big rocket, Ariane 6, was meant to fly on 23 November. But the launch team stopped the [[countdown|countdown]].
Some equipment on the ground had a problem. The rocket and its 36 internet [[satellite|satellites]] are safe.
Launch teams always stop when something is not right. The team will try again on 24 November or later. Then the satellites can go into [[orbit|orbit]] and send internet signals to Earth.

o.t: Ariane 6 launch with 36 internet satellites is put on hold
b: Arianespace, the company running the launch, stopped the [[countdown|countdown]] for Ariane 6 flight VA271 on Monday 23 November. The rocket was due to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, [[french-guiana|French Guiana]], carrying 36 Amazon Leo internet [[satellite|satellites]].

The cause was a technical issue with the rocket's ground support systems, the equipment on the ground that helps get a rocket ready to fly. The countdown stopped before the mobile [[gantry|gantry]], a tall movable tower around the rocket, had been taken away. Arianespace said the rocket and the satellites remain stable and safe.

Launch teams halt a countdown whenever anything is not right, because safety comes first. A delay like this is normal, not a failure. The next attempt will be no earlier than 24 November. Once launched, the satellites will go into [[orbit|orbit]] and send internet signals down to places on Earth.

stories.think: Can you think of a time when stopping to check something was the smart thing to do?

quiz.q: Why did the Ariane 6 countdown stop?
a: A storm over the launch site
A problem with equipment on the ground
The rocket ran out of fuel

x.t: India and Nepal start a new train and open a bridge
b: India and Nepal are neighbours. Their leaders met in New Delhi on Monday.
Together they started a new train. It runs between Ayodhya in India and Janakpur in Nepal. A new road bridge across the border was opened too.
The two countries also signed eight [[mou|agreements]]. These are written plans to work together.

o.t: India and Nepal sign eight agreements and launch a new train
b: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah visited India on 22 and 23 November. On Monday he held talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, and the two countries signed eight [[mou|MoUs]], or memorandums of understanding: written agreements on how they plan to work together.

One MoU, between [[isro|ISRO]], India's space agency, and Nepal's communications ministry, will set up a [[satellite|satellite]] communication network using the South Asia Satellite. Others cover Ayurveda and traditional medicine, sustainable urban development (planning cities that can grow without harming nature), and livestock and fisheries.

The leaders also launched the Saryu-Kamala Express, a train between Ayodhya in India and Janakpur in Nepal. A road bridge linking Dharchula in India and Darchula in Nepal was opened. The foundation stone, which marks the start of building, was laid for the 669 MW Lower Arun [[hydroelectric|Hydroelectric]] Project. India also announced a package to help Nepal rebuild after floods.

x.t: Is there a hidden planet far past Neptune?
b: Some scientists think a hidden planet may circle the Sun far past [[neptune|Neptune]]. Nobody has seen it yet. It is just an idea.
The idea comes from computer [[simulation|models]]. They replayed 4.5 billion years of the Sun and its planets. They point to a planet heavier than Earth.
Next, a big telescope that scans the sky could help check. That is how science works: guess, then check.

o.t: Could a hidden planet be orbiting far beyond Neptune?
b: Astronomers suggest a planet nicknamed "Planet X2" may [[orbit|orbit]] the Sun far beyond [[neptune|Neptune]]. It would have about 1.5 to 2 times Earth's mass. It has not been observed: it is a hypothesis, an untested idea.

The idea comes from computer [[simulation|simulations]], models that imitate real things, covering 4.5 billion years of Solar System history. The planet's average distance from the Sun would be about 350 to 500 [[astronomical-unit|astronomical units]] (AU). One AU is Earth's average distance from the Sun. It could explain the unusual orbits of [[trans-neptunian-object|trans-Neptunian objects]], distant icy objects past Neptune.

The study, led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka of Kindai University, Japan, is in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. "If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our Solar System," Lykawka said. Next, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's sky survey could help test the idea.

stories.think: If you cannot see something, what clues could tell you it might be there?

quiz.q: Where does the idea of Planet X2 come from?
a: A photo taken by a telescope
A visit by a space probe

x.t: Share prices in India go down after a run of gains
b: A [[share|share]] is a tiny piece of a company. People buy and sell shares every day.
The [[sensex|Sensex]] is like a score for the share prices of big companies. On Monday, the Sensex went down.
Many people sold shares after prices had gone up. Bank shares fell the most. Prices go up and down every day. People will keep buying and selling.

o.t: Sensex and Nifty fall as investors sell bank shares
b: India's main share indexes, the [[sensex|Sensex]] and the [[nifty|Nifty]], fell on Monday 23 November. The Sensex dropped 1,483.72 points, or 1.77%, to 82,435.99. The Nifty fell 450.95 points, or 1.75%, to 25,349.65.

A [[share|share]] is a small piece of a company, and its price changes as people buy and sell. An index is like an average score for the share prices of big companies. Bank and financial company shares led Monday's fall, as many investors sold to [[profit-taking|take profits]] after recent gains.

Markets in other countries also fell. South Korea's main index, the KOSPI, closed about 3.3% lower on Monday, and the US Nasdaq index fell about 5.3% on Friday. Around the world, shares of companies linked to [[ai|artificial intelligence]] have also fallen. Prices rise and fall every day, and investors will keep watching.

stories.think: If you owned a tiny piece of a company, what would make you want to keep it or sell it?

quiz.q: Which shares led the fall in India on Monday?

x.t: Wild otters make a home in a big city river
b: Wild otters are living in a river in Kuala Lumpur. Kuala Lumpur is a big city in Malaysia.
Otters eat fish. So otters in a river mean there are probably fish there too. That suggests the [[klang-river|river]] is getting healthier.
People have been working hard to clean the river. Machines powered by the sun help catch rubbish. Otters are now seen more often.

o.t: Otters in Kuala Lumpur's river are a sign the clean-up is working
b: Wild otters are living along the [[klang-river|Klang River]] in Kuala Lumpur, a big city in Malaysia. Conservationists, people who work to protect nature, see the otters as a sign that work to clean up the river is helping.

Woo Chee Yoong is a co-founder of the Malaysian Otter Network, a group that works to protect otters. He says the otters being there suggests there are fish in the river, because otters need fish to eat.

Otters are now being seen more and more often in Kuala Lumpur. Part of the clean-up uses solar-powered machines called [[interceptor|Interceptors]], from a Dutch non-profit group (an organisation that does not aim to make money), which collect rubbish from the river. Each new sighting gives scientists another clue about how healthy the river is becoming.

stories.think: If you could help clean up one place near your home, which would you choose and why?

quiz.q: Why is seeing otters in the river good news?
a: It suggests there are fish in the river

orbit: The path something follows as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like the Sun.
The curved path that an object in space follows as it moves around a planet, star or moon.
tiangong: China's space station, where astronauts live and do science.

payload-specialist: An astronaut who goes to space to do science work.
A crew member on a space mission whose main job is to carry out experiments or other science work.
space-station: A big spacecraft that stays in space. Astronauts live and work there.
A large spacecraft that stays in orbit for years, where crews live and work and do experiments.

test-draw: When a match ends and nobody wins.
In Test cricket, the result when a match ends before either team has won.
declare: In cricket, when a team chooses to stop batting early.
In cricket, to choose to end your team's innings before all of its batters are out.
century: A score of 100 runs or more by one player.
In cricket, a score of 100 runs or more by one player in one innings.
over: In cricket, a set of balls bowled by one bowler.
In cricket, a set of balls bowled in a row by one bowler. Counting overs shows how long a team has batted.
mou: A written plan to work together.
A memorandum of understanding: a written agreement that sets out how two sides plan to work together.
isro: The Indian Space Research Organisation, India's space agency.
satellite: A machine sent into space that travels around Earth.
A machine that is sent into space and moves around Earth or another planet.
hydroelectric: Describes electricity made by using the force of moving water to turn machines. MW, or megawatts, measures how much power a plant can make.
share: A tiny piece of a company that people can buy.
One of the equal parts a company is divided into. People who own shares own a small part of the company, and share prices change as people buy and sell.
sensex: A number that shows how the share prices of big Indian companies are doing.
An index of share prices on the Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai. When it goes down, the prices of the shares it follows have fallen on average.
nifty: Another number that shows how the share prices of big Indian companies are doing.
Another major Indian share index. Like the Sensex, it follows the share prices of a group of big companies.
profit-taking: To sell something after its price has gone up.
To sell shares after their price has risen, so that the seller keeps the gain.
ai: Computer systems that can copy clever things that people do.
Computer systems that can copy intelligent human behaviour. The term also means the study and development of these systems.
countdown: Counting down the time and doing checks before a rocket takes off.
The planned series of steps and checks, counted down in time, that a launch team works through before a rocket lifts off.
french-guiana: A place in South America where Europe launches rockets.
A region of France on the north-east coast of South America, home to Europe's Spaceport in Kourou.
gantry: A tall tower that stands around a rocket before it flies.
A tall structure built around a rocket on the launch pad so workers can reach it; a mobile gantry is moved away before launch.
klang-river: A river that flows through the city of Kuala Lumpur.
A river in Malaysia that runs through the city of Kuala Lumpur.
interceptor: A machine in a river that catches rubbish.
A solar-powered machine, from a Dutch non-profit group, that collects rubbish floating in a river.
neptune: A planet far out in our Solar System.
One of the planets that travel around the Sun, far out in the Solar System.
simulation: A practice run that copies the real thing, sometimes on a computer.
A model, often on a computer, that imitates something real, so that an idea can be tested without doing it for real.
astronomical-unit: A way to measure huge distances in space. One is as far as Earth is from the Sun.
A unit for measuring distances in space: 1 AU is the average distance from Earth to the Sun.
trans-neptunian-object: An icy object in space, far past Neptune.
Any small, icy object that travels around the Sun beyond the orbit of Neptune.

days.name: Fibonacci Day
days.what: Fibonacci Day honours Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, and the number pattern named after him. In the Fibonacci sequence, each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on. Written month first, the date 11/23 shows 1, 1, 2, 3. Fibonacci described the sequence in 1202 and helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe.

learn.subject: Science
learn.link: From the bird flu vaccine story: a vaccine helps a body learn to protect itself

x.t: How a vaccine trains the body
b: Some germs can make people and animals ill. India has made a new vaccine to protect chickens from bird flu.
A vaccine has germs that are made weak or switched off. Some vaccines have just a small part of a germ. These do not make you ill.
The body learns to spot the germ. It makes antibodies, tiny helpers that fight the germ. It also remembers the germ, so it can act fast next time.
x.remember: A vaccine teaches the body to spot a germ, so it is ready to fight it next time.
x.q: What does a vaccine teach the body to do?
a: Spot a germ and fight it

o.t: How does a vaccine train the body to protect itself?
b: A vaccine helps the body get ready for a germ before it meets the real thing. Most vaccines contain a weakened or inactive form of a germ, such as a virus or bacterium, or a small part of one. This part is called an antigen: something the body's defences can recognise. Some newer vaccines carry instructions that let the body make the antigen itself.

The immune system is the body's defence system. Its immune cells make antibodies, which are proteins that recognise a particular antigen and help fight it. The first time the body meets an antigen, it needs time to make the right antibodies. A vaccine lets this happen without the dangers of a real illness.

Afterwards, the immune system keeps a memory of the germ. If the real germ arrives later, the body can make the right antibodies quickly. Vaccines are used for animals as well as people: India's new bird flu vaccine is meant to protect chickens.
o.remember: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of a germ, so it can remember the germ and respond quickly later.
o.q: What happens if the real germ arrives after a vaccine has done its work?
a: The body makes the right antibodies quickly
The vaccine turns into the germ

backThen.t: Doctor Who is shown on television for the first time
backThen.o: On 23 November 1963, the BBC showed the first episode of Doctor Who on television in the United Kingdom. The episode was called An Unearthly Child. The programme was cancelled in 1989, but it came back in 2005.
backThen.x: On this day in 1963, the first episode of Doctor Who was shown on TV in the UK. The BBC made it. The show stopped in 1989. It came back in 2005.
backThen.why: A television programme can stop and still return: Doctor Who came back in 2005, 16 years after it was cancelled.

hiddenWords.o: Orbit comes from the Latin word orbita, which means a wheel track or path. The Romans also used it for the path of a heavenly body through the sky.
Tournament comes from the Old French word torneiement, which became tornement in Middle English. It meant a contest between two teams of knights on horseback.
